name: Henry VIII of England
summary: An absolute-minded Tudor monarch whose recorded positions centre on royal and national sovereignty: he broke with Rome, made himself supreme head of the English church, and enforced doctrinal conformity and loyalty by treason law and execution. His written record is mostly statutes and one late speech urging charity in religious dispute, so economic and social questions are largely unaddressed.

property-fundamental.rationale: Dissolved the monasteries and took their land, and used attainders to seize property.

state-harmful.rationale: Appeals preamble presents the crown's justice as preserving unity and peace and the realm as an empire under one head.

empower-police-military.rationale: Personally enlarged the royal fleet and dockyards and ordered sustained military enforcement after rebellion.

decide-locally.rationale: Centralised power by abolishing marcher lordships and bringing Wales and the church under one national system.

rehabilitation.rationale: No recorded position on what prisons should aim at; executions for treason and heresy are about something nearby.

more-religion-public.rationale: Prescribed uniform Christian instruction and conduct under royal supervision.

revolution-justified.rationale: Treated the Pilgrimage of Grace as treason and made denying royal supremacy treason.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Personally expanded royal shipbuilding through new dockyards, supply facilities and naval administration.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Appeals Act preamble describes England as an empire governed by one supreme head and king with plenary power from God.

democracy-best.rationale: Declared ordinary commoners unqualified to choose councillors or direct the affairs reserved to their prince.

natural-rulers.rationale: Distinguished the prince and selected nobles’ capacity to rule from commoners’ alleged incapacity; not a biological theory.

political-violence-never.rationale: Agreed to a plot to kill Cardinal Beaton despite condemning domestic rebellion; his connection to the final murder is less certain.

separate-church-state.rationale: Made himself and his successors the only supreme head of the Church of England, with power to reform doctrine and correct errors, annexed to the crown.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Rested his annulment case on Leviticus and passed doctrine into statute, but also relied on royal and parliamentary authority; mixed evidence.

military-superiority.rationale: Founded a permanent navy and expanded it from seven to up to 50 ships.

taxation-theft.rationale: Defended parliamentary subsidies and first-fruits as legitimate contributions subjects owed toward government and defense.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Invaded France in 1512 and 1544 seeking to recover territory, took Boulogne, and attacked Scotland; also annexed Wales and became King of Ireland in 1542.

national-self-determination.rationale: Claimed English sovereignty over Scotland through hereditary right and homage, rather than Scottish national choice.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Faith explicitly subordinates natural reason to religious knowledge.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Personally drove religious-conformity legislation, extending government beyond defense, justice and property protection.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Law punished abandoning the established doctrine in either direction (Six Articles for reformers, Treasons Act for those denying supremacy); not framed as a conversion law.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Grounded subjects’ obligatory allegiance in divine command and nature, rejecting their claim to control government.

population-transfer.rationale: Pursued an English colony through displacement of the native French population and restrictions on return.

separated-powers.rationale: Creed and Commandment VI deny independent authorities above kings.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Used attainder by Parliament instead of trial against Cromwell and others, and broke the pardon given to the Pilgrimage of Grace rebels.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Took personal command at Boulogne in 1544, built a permanent navy, and appointed and dismissed his own ministers such as Cromwell.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Kept episcopal government: bishops were nominated by the king and the Six Articles and King's Book kept traditional hierarchy and sacraments.

clerical-rule.rationale: Placed clergy beneath the crown and told them in his last speech to amend or he would correct them as God's vicar.

death-penalty.rationale: Capital punishment for treason and heresy was routine, including burning and hanging under the Six Articles and Treasons Act.

minority-language-support.rationale: Act imposed English law and the English language on Welsh-speaking Wales.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Successive acts settled the crown by heredity; Supremacy Act annexes headship to the crown for his heirs and successors.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Acts of Appeals and Supremacy put the clergy under crown authority, and the Suppression Acts dissolved the monasteries and took their property.

region-keeps-system.rationale: The Laws in Wales Acts abolished the marcher lordships and replaced Welsh arrangements with English law and administration.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Claimed to be God's vicar and supreme head of the church, but nothing recorded claims divine descent; mixed.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Claimed plenary power and used attainders, yet acted through Parliament for the great changes; contested.

refugee-return.rationale: Barred displaced inhabitants’ return to lands claimed by conquest, prioritizing English settlement in the Boulonnais.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Statutory penalties up to burning for rejecting the articles of faith set by the crown; denying the established doctrine was a capital offence.

ban-cartels.rationale: Inferred: VIII condemns monopolization; V requires princely moral enforcement.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Preserved hereditary royal succession and governed through nobles rather than abolishing inherited rank.

elective-rulers.rationale: Succession Acts settled the throne by inheritance among his children, not by election.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Made it treason to call the king tyrant, heretic or usurper and executed the Pilgrimage of Grace leaders.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Used Parliament to enact the Reformation but held that the king was supreme head with full authority; contested.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Commandment VIII requires owners to aid needy neighbours.

return-lost-territory.rationale: His French campaigns aimed at recovering Aquitaine and ruling France.

filial-duty.rationale: Commandment V requires lifelong parental respect and material support.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Turned to Parliament for subsidies yet also raised money by debasement and monastic lands without parliamentary vote.

single-official-language.rationale: The 1535 Act applied English law and administration in Wales and required the English language in them.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Appeals preamble says all subjects owe the king natural and humble obedience; refusal of oaths and statutes was made treason.

non-intervention.rationale: Claimed authority over Scotland and personally directed military coercion of its rulers and population.

religious-nation.rationale: Appeals preamble treats the realm as one body politic of spiritualty and temporalty; he demanded doctrinal uniformity and an oath of supremacy of all adults.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: Explicitly required Scottish kings to recognize English superiority through homage and fealty.

majority-settlement.rationale: Personally wanted an ethnically English colony in conquered territory, populated by English farmers and soldiers.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: The Buggery Act 1533, passed in his reign through Cromwell, made sodomy a statutory offence; its term was not defined in the text.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Treasons Act 1534 criminalised words against supremacy; executed More, Fisher and the Pilgrimage of Grace leaders despite a promised pardon.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Supremacy Act aimed to repress heresies; the Six Articles act punished denial of transubstantiation by burning and other denials by hanging or imprisonment.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: His colonial project used conquered farmland and resources to extend English royal control and reward English settlers.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Appeals preamble says the king is furnished by Almighty God with plenary power; in his last speech he called himself God's appointed vicar and high minister.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Drove the Succession Acts (1533, 1536, 1543) fixing succession among his children and, in 1543, gaining power to settle it by will.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Commandment VI expressly permits lawful self-defense and public punishment.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Provided publicly endowed masses, preaching and charitable support alongside his own explicitly spiritual account of human destiny.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Began wars with France in 1512 and 1544 and the 'Rough Wooing' of Scotland.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Fixed one official doctrine by statute with severe penalties (Six Articles 1539, King's Book 1543) and exhorted subjects to end religious division on his terms.

premarital-sex.rationale: Commandment VII condemns fornication and sexual infidelity.

national-church-status.rationale: Created the Church of England under the crown and enforced its doctrine by statute (Six Articles, King's Book).

distribution-by-process.rationale: Inferred: VIII and X distinguish lawful wealth from fraudulent acquisition.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: Mixed: the King's Book (Commandment V) exempts commands contrary to God from obedience, but he executed subjects such as Thomas More and John Fisher who refused his laws on conscience.

notes:
Religious views changed: he defended papal authority and the sacraments in the Assertio Septem Sacramentorum (1521, not read in full here), then broke with Rome in 1533-34 while keeping traditional doctrine in the Six Articles and King's Book. Answers use his mature position. Full texts of the Six Articles act, Ten Articles, King's Book and Letters and Papers were not retrieved; those are described through reference summaries.

Merged with an independent gpt-6.1-sol audit: 27 answers taken from it, 24 agreed, 0 conflicts settled by the integrator.

gpt-6.1-sol notes: Independent pass: previous answers were not consulted. Whole active list and remaining nulls reviewed. The 1543 doctrinal book was collaboratively prepared, personally revised and explicitly endorsed by Henry; individual sections are cited without claiming he authored every sentence. Mature religion is distinguished from his earlier papal allegiance. Six Articles evidence includes the preamble’s specific account of his personal intervention, not royal assent alone. Ordinary statutes concerning Wales, Irish clothing, sodomy, poor relief, usury or prices are not automatically attributed to him. Economic searches included a full monetary-history article and the accessible scholarly extract and references on food-price proclamations; government action without personal involvement is insufficient. Sovereign coin debasement does not itself answer modern public-versus-private bank-credit creation, deficit stimulus or central-bank independence. Moral usury language is insufficient for a current blanket interest prohibition, particularly given the later 1545 statute. Threats and exemplary execution orders are attributed to him; the historians explicitly doubt whether every order was implemented. Beaton plotting concerns extralegal assassination, not ordinary state warfare; the identity of an intermediary and the connection of earlier plots to the final killing remain disputed. Colonial officers’ independent abuses are distinguished from Henry’s policy: attacks on departing Boulogne civilians violated his initial safe-conduct orders. The later settlement program nevertheless explicitly sought an ethnically English colony; the follow-up historian attributes this aim to Henry personally. A colonial ethnic-settlement policy does not by itself establish that all nations must consist mainly of one ethnic group. Black court musician John Blanke’s employment and wedding gifts do not establish Henry’s general position on racial equality or interracial marriage. No biological racial theory, class theory of history, third-way economics or view that competition drives progress was found. The legendary Brutus genealogy supports a royal territorial claim, but is not automatically a modern doctrine of national identity. Religious conformity does not itself define national membership by religion. Sacramental theology does not establish literal interpretation of every scriptural passage. Views on slavery, modern technology, climate and universal healthcare are not invented from Tudor institutions. The portrait commission was for a restricted palace audience and does not alone demonstrate a public mass leader cult. Naval construction is strategic state investment, not proof that all major industries should be publicly owned. Only rationales starting Inferred: are historical inferences.
